headline: A Michigan Democrat backed the Republican.
summary: Rep. Haley Stevens lost Michigan's Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in August. On Sunday, two days before the election, she stood beside Republican Mike Rogers at a Detroit church and endorsed him. El-Sayed had uninvited her from his own event that morning after a fight over an ad about Israel. Her chief of staff quit.

cover_question.q: Why did she pick the other team?

cover_answer: They had a fight, and he told her to stay away.
table_question: If your team cut you, would you play for the other side?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Two people on the same team wanted the same job in Michigan, and a summer vote picked Abdul El-Sayed. Haley Stevens lost, and later he told her she wasn't welcome on his team. So on Sunday she picked the other team's player, like leaving kickball after a fight to play for the other side. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Teams, a vote, a fight, a switch: four things a six-year-old has seen at recess. The names stay because a real person holds better.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script makes it the switch: she lost the vote, got told to stay away, and went to the other side. Kickball is the anchor: recess has all four parts. Expect "is she a bad guy now?" Say no, she picked a side after a fight, and grown-ups are still arguing about it.

8-12.script: Haley Stevens lost Michigan's Democratic Senate primary in August and backed the winner, Abdul El-Sayed. Then they fought over an ad, he told her to stay away, and on Sunday she endorsed his Republican rival, Mike Rogers. Like losing the captain vote and joining the other team.
8-12.why: A five-step chain they can follow, and the captain vote puts it on a playground they know.
8-12.why_long: This age is testing whether adults keep their word, and this story is about one who didn't: she said she would back the nominee, then endorsed his rival. The captain vote puts a five-step chain on a field they know. Expect "can she even do that?" Say yes, anyone can endorse anyone, then ask whether her reason is good enough.

13-17.script: Haley Stevens says she is not turning her back on Democrats: "It is this one vote." Her chief of staff quit anyway. Is one vote ever just one vote for a congresswoman? Second: El-Sayed's campaign told her to stay away, and she endorsed his rival the same day. Who broke the team first?
13-17.why: Both questions have a real answer on each side. Her own quote is the honest place to start.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: he uninvited her, and she had spent the week demanding he pull two ads. Kuhn calls argument a skill that is practised, and "who broke the team first" has evidence on both sides. Expect "why does the aide quitting matter?" Say the aide thought one vote was never just one, then ask them.

5-7.q: Why did she pick the other team?
5-7.a: They had a fight, and he said stay away. So she chose the other side.

8-12.q: Is she allowed to do that?
8-12.a: Yes. Anyone can endorse anyone. Her party is angry and her aide quit.
Nobody knows until Tuesday. The seat could decide who runs the Senate.

13-17.a: Argue it. He uninvited her; she had already demanded he pull two ads.

13-17.q: Is one vote ever just one vote for a congresswoman?
13-17.a: Her chief of staff didn't think so. Ask what the aide saw that she didn't.
